item.title: “For the most part, monks, beings find pleasure in sensual pleasures. But a clansman who has set aside the sickle and the carrying-pole, gone forth…
item.description:
“For the most part, monks, beings find pleasure in sensual pleasures. But a clansman who has set aside the sickle and the carrying-pole, gone forth from the household life into homelessness, is justifiably called ‘a clansman who has gone forth out of faith.’ Why is that? Sensual pleasures are found with youth, these sensual pleasures or others. And, monks, low sensual pleasures, middling sensual pleasures, and supreme sensual pleasures — all are classed as sensual pleasures.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.7

item.title: “Monks, sensual pleasures are impermanent, empty, false, of a delusive nature. Monks, this is the mere greeting of a fool built upon deception. Sensual pleasures…
item.description:
“Monks, sensual pleasures are impermanent, empty, false, of a delusive nature. Monks, this is the mere greeting of a fool built upon deception. Sensual pleasures present and future, perceptions of sensual pleasure present and future — both belong to Māra’s realm, Māra’s domain, Māra’s bait, Māra’s food.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 106 – Āneñjasappāyasutta

item.title: “Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. This, good sirs, is called suffering. Good sirs, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, good sirs, is called the origin of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta

item.title: “Venerable Gotama, I have a perplexity and doubt: ‘How should one understand the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama?’” - “Vaccha, your perplexity is enough, your…
item.description:
“Venerable Gotama, I have a perplexity and doubt: ‘How should one understand the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama?’” - “Vaccha, your perplexity is enough, your doubt is enough. It is on this point that perplexity and doubt have arisen. I declare the rebirth of one who has clinging, Vaccha, not of one who has no clinging. Just as, Vaccha, a fire burns when there is fuel, not when there is no fuel. So too, Vaccha, I declare rebirth for one who has clinging, not for one who has no clinging.” - “Venerable Gotama, when the wind blows a fire far away, what does Venerable Gotama declare as the fuel for that fire?” - “Vaccha, when the wind blows a fire far away, I say that the wind is its fuel. At that time, Vaccha, the wind is the fuel (upādāna).” - “Venerable Gotama, when a being gives up this body and is reborn in another body, what does Venerable Gotama declare as the fuel for that being?” - “Vaccha, when a being gives up this body and is reborn in another body, I declare that at that time craving (taṇhā) is the fuel (upādāna).”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 44.9

item.title: “Householder, suppose near a village or town there is a forest grove. In it there is a tree full of ripe fruits, but none have…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose near a village or town there is a forest grove. In it there is a tree full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen to the ground. Then a man comes, wishing for fruit, seeking fruit, wandering here and there for fruit. He enters that forest, sees that tree full of ripe fruits, and thinks: ‘This tree is full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen. I know how to climb trees. Suppose I climb this tree, eat my fill, and fill my clothes.’ Then he climbs the tree, eats his fill, and fills his clothes. Then a second man comes, wishing for fruit, seeking fruit, wandering here and there for fruit, carrying a sharp axe. He enters that forest, sees that tree full of ripe fruits, and thinks: ‘This tree is full of ripe fruits, but none have fallen. I don’t know how to climb trees. Suppose I cut this tree down at the root, eat my fill, and fill my clothes.’ Then he cuts the tree down at the root. What do you think, householder? If the first man does not climb down quickly, when the tree falls, will it not break his hand, foot, or some part of his body, and will he not thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a fruit tree — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: “Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The…
item.description:
“Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The mind arises first for those things, and the unwholesome states follow after.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.56

item.title: “Monks, short indeed is the lifespan of humans in this world — one must go on to the future. Do good, live the holy life.…
item.description:
“Monks, short indeed is the lifespan of humans in this world — one must go on to the future. Do good, live the holy life. For nothing that is born is without death. Monks, a long-lived person lives only a hundred years, or a little more or less.

Human life is short,
The good person should be concerned,
Live as if the head is on fire —
Death will surely come.

Days and nights pass by,
Life span comes to an end,
Human life dries up
Like a stream in the mountains.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.9
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that…
item.description:
“He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had delusion — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome.’ Thus, in this very life, he is freed from longing, calm, cooled, experiencing ease, abiding in the Brahma-state himself.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66

item.title: “Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all unarisen evil, unwholesome states are not yet abandoned within him, then he should arouse…
item.description:
“Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all unarisen evil, unwholesome states are not yet abandoned within him, then he should arouse energy to abandon those evil, unwholesome states. Good sirs, if, while reflecting, a monk sees clearly that all evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned within him, then he should dwell with joyful mind, training in wholesome states day and night.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 15 – Anumānasutta

item.title: Elder Puṇṇamāsa: Having abandoned the five hindrances, Attaining security from bondage, Holding the mirror of the Dhamma, Knowing and seeing the self. I contemplate this…
item.description:
Elder Puṇṇamāsa:

Having abandoned the five hindrances,
Attaining security from bondage,
Holding the mirror of the Dhamma,
Knowing and seeing the self.

I contemplate this body,
From within and without —
The body is seen as empty,
Both inside and out.

From: Theragāthā 2.26
